site.name: The 9% Club
site.tagline: Most traders lose money. Here's the arithmetic.

ch00.title:
You have ₹2,000.

Let's buy a business.
ch00.tagline: Before any of the trading, charts or jargon: what are you actually buying when you buy a share? Start here.
ch00.outroH: That is all a share is.
ch00.outroP: A share is a slice of a real business. Not a lottery ticket, not a number on a screen. When the business does well your slice is worth more. When it does badly, your slice is worth less. You carry both.
ch00.handoffQ: So you want your ₹2,000 back. Who buys your tokens?
ch00.handoffP: You have to find a person, agree a price, and trust them to pay. That problem is the entire reason stock exchanges exist. That is Chapter 01.

beats.p: Aarti and Imran want to run a cold coffee cart outside the station, where four thousand students walk past every evening.
An espresso machine, a commercial blender, the cart itself, and a month of beans and milk. They have ₹40,000 between them.

beats.h: So they split the cart into 100 pieces.
beats.p: One hundred tokens, ₹1,000 each. Buy a token and you own one hundredth of the business. Not a loan. Ownership.
Your ₹2,000 becomes 2% of a coffee cart. That is it. That is the whole idea behind owning a share.

beats.h: The money becomes a real thing.
beats.p: Your ₹2,000 is not sitting in an app. It is a wheel, a steel counter, part of an espresso machine. Shares are claims on real objects and real work.
They sell 240 cups a day at ₹80. After beans, milk, ice and the pitch fee, the cart clears about ₹1,20,000 over the season.
You did not make a single cup. You own 2% of the business, so you own 2% of what it earned. Your ₹2,000 is now worth about ₹4,400.

beats.h: June. It rains for nine days straight.
beats.p: Nobody queues for cold coffee in the rain. Sales fall to 30 cups a day. Milk spoils. The rent on the pitch is due anyway.
This is the part the reels leave out. Ownership is not a one way street. The same 2% that earned you the summer carries the monsoon.

beats.h: You own a business, not a bet.
beats.p: Over a year the cart made money. Not every month, and not without two months that genuinely hurt. Your slice followed it the whole way, up and down.

ch00.cartAlt: An isometric coffee cart assembling itself
ch00.gridAlt: One hundred ownership tokens, two of them yours

nav.label: Chapters
nav.endNote: That is the whole course: what a share is, how a trade travels, what it costs, what a fall feels like, why most traders lose, and what boring looks like. All of it is arithmetic and history. None of it is advice.

ch04.title:
What a trade

really costs.
ch04.tagline: Your shares closed at ₹103, but set that aside. To see what a trade costs on its own, take the price out of it: back to {wallet}, and nothing in this chapter needs a price to move.
ch04.noteAlt: A {trade} note with each charge cut off its end, drawn to scale
ch04.zoomNote: The note is to scale. These bars are zoomed in, or you could not see them.

beats.p: The counter resets so the charges have nothing to hide behind. Same app, same ₹100 share, and this time the price stays still.
{qty} shares at {price} each. Later you sell all {qty} at the same {price}. From here the counter follows only this {trade}, because this is the money the charges touch.

A broker is the company whose app places your order. This one takes {brokerageLeg} when you buy and {brokerageLeg} when you sell. Some apps advertise zero brokerage, but every cut after this one still comes.

Your shares sit in a demat account, a locker for shares. Each time you sell, you pay this DP charge to take them out. It stays {dp} whatever the trade size, so here it alone eats {dpPct}% of your money.
STT is Securities Transaction Tax, a tax on buying and selling shares. {sttLeg} on the way in, {sttLeg} on the way out. No app can waive it.
The exchange, where orders meet: {exchange}. SEBI, the market regulator: {sebi}. Stamp duty on the purchase: {stamp}. GST on the broker's and exchange's fees: {gst}.

beats.h: The share did not move. You are down {lostPct}%.
beats.p: You bought at {price} and sold at {price}. Of your {trade}, {kept} came back. The other {total} is that pile of slices.

ch04.outroP: A price can go up or down. These charges only go one way, and they come whatever the price does.
ch04.handoffQ: So how far must a price rise just to get your money back?
ch04.handoffP: On {trade} it is {lostPct}%. Does the amount you trade change that? Chapter 05 is that arithmetic.
ch04.assumptions: Worked for a delivery trade on NSE, meaning shares bought and held at least overnight, using statutory rates checked in November 2026 and a conservative reading of one discount broker's fees. Rates change, so your own contract note may differ.

ch05.title:
Why ₹2,000

cannot trade.
ch05.tagline: This is arithmetic, not advice. You start again with {wallet}, and there is one question: how far must a price rise before a trade simply gets your money back?
ch05.chartAlt: Bars showing the breakeven gap shrinking from {pct500}% at {c500} to {pct50000}% at {c50000}

beats.p: Buy a share, sell it, pay the charges. The breakeven gap is how far the price must rise for you to end with exactly what you started with. No profit. Just your money back.
Charges on one round trip come to {cost500}. On an amount this small, the price has a long way to climb.
This is the trade from Chapter 04, with {cost1000} in charges. Double the money and the gap nearly halves.
A round trip costs {cost2000}. The share has to rise nearly 2% before you have earned a single rupee.
The dark part of each bar is the DP charge. It does not care how much you trade, and at {c2000} it is {dpShare}% of your charges. The smaller the trade, the taller it stands.
{ten} round trips of {c2000}, with the price never moving, cost about {tenCost}. That is {tenPct}% of your money gone, before any trade has gone right or wrong.
The same {dp}, spread over more money. Charges are {cost5000}, and the gap is less than half of yours.
Charges are {cost10000}. The wall is fading, because more of the bill now grows with the trade instead of staying flat.
Less than a fifth of your gap. It is still a gap, though, and clearing it only gets you back to zero.
Slide the amount. These figures come from the same calculation as every number on this page. They show the cost of one round trip, not what any price will do.

ch05.outroH: The gap is not a prediction.
ch05.outroP: It says nothing about where any price is going. It only measures how far a price has to travel before one trade pays for itself, and at {wallet} that distance is long for reasons that have nothing to do with skill.
ch05.assumptions: One delivery round trip on NSE at the same buy and sell price, which slightly understates the true gap, since sell-side charges grow with a higher exit price. The ten-trade figure keeps the trade size fixed at ₹2,000 for simplicity. Statutory rates checked in November 2026, with a conservative reading of one discount broker's fees. This is education, not advice.

ch06.title:
What losing

looks like.
ch06.tagline: The cart was invented. This is not. Back to {wallet}, on a real line from a real crash, and at the worst moment you get to choose.
ch06.crashAlt: The real curve falling {fallPct}% in {fallDays} days, from {wallet} to {bottom}
ch06.fullAlt: The real curve recovering after the fall and ending near {final}, against a flat line at {bottomRound} for selling at the bottom

beats.p: 11 February 2020. Your {wallet} is spread evenly across 49 large Indian companies. No story this time: every point on this line happened.

beats.h: It starts as a bad week.
beats.p: A few red days. Then more. Nothing on the screen tells you how far this will go, and everyone you ask sounds certain, in both directions.
March 2020. Lockdown news, every screen red. Nobody did anything wrong. Your {wallet} is now {bottom}.
24 March 2020. This turned out to be the bottom, but nobody could know that today. Choose as if you do not know what comes next, then keep scrolling.

beats.h: {recoverDays} days later, the line was back.
beats.p: By August 2020 it had climbed past where it started. Anyone who sold stayed at {bottomRound}. Selling is what turns a fall on a screen into a real loss.
By the end of 2025, and not smoothly: there was another steep fall on the way. Held, {bottom} became {final}. Sold, it stayed {bottomRound}.
The gap between {final} and {bottomRound} did not come from skill or a better pick. It came from what someone did during one frightening week.

beats.h: This is one crash, not a rule.
beats.p: Nobody is promised a recovery, or one this fast. This basket also leaves out companies that collapsed, which flatters the gain. The lesson is how a loss feels, and what selling does to it. It is not that holding always wins.

ch06.outroH: A fall hurts before it is real.
ch06.outroP: Most of what losing feels like happens before you sell. Knowing that in advance will not make it pleasant, but it is the only preparation there is.
ch06.assumptions: Real prices, 2019 to 2025: 49 large Indian companies bought in equal weight in January 2019 and not rebalanced. The list is made of companies that are large today, so ones that failed are missing, and that flatters the result. The steep fall in early 2023 came mainly from one holding growing too large in the basket, not from the wider market, which is why this chapter teaches from 2020. Charges and tax are left out. Rupee figures are the basket's movement applied to {wallet}, starting at the February 2020 high. Past prices say nothing about future ones. This is education, not advice.

ch07.title:
The 91%

number, FY25.
ch07.tagline: This is where the name comes from. It is a count of what happened to real people, and it is not an invitation to be one of the {kept}.
ch07.gridAlt: One hundred figures, of which {lost} go dark and {kept} remain
ch07.countLabel: lost money in FY25, after charges
ch07.lossLabel: net loss of individual F&O traders, FY25

beats.p: They trade futures and options, or F&O: contracts that bet on where a price goes, where a small deposit controls a much bigger amount. Each one expects to be the exception.
SEBI, the market regulator, went through individual traders' F&O records for 2024-25. Not a survey and not an opinion. What actually happened to their money.

beats.h: In FY25, {lost} of them lost money.
beats.p: After charges, {lost} in every 100 individual traders ended the year with a net loss.
That is the number in the name. It is not a club with a way in, and this site does not offer one. Being among the {kept} in one year says nothing about the next.

Chapters 04 and 05 showed charges arriving before a price moves. F&O has its own charges, different from a delivery trade, but the arithmetic is the same: every trade pays, right or wrong, and more trades pay more.
Selling in a panic. Trading again to win it back. Each extra trade pays charges again. An earlier SEBI study found more than 75% of loss-makers kept trading after consecutive years of losses.
That is what individual traders lost together in 2024-25, after charges. One crore is ₹1,00,00,000. Behind that number are students, salaries and savings.

beats.h: A year later, a similar picture.
beats.p: SEBI's next study, published in August 2026, found that {fy26Pct}% of individual F&O traders lost money in FY26, with net losses of {fy26Loss} crore. SEBI itself cautions that 20% fewer people traded that year, so a smaller share of losers does not mean trading got better.

beats.h: If you lost money, you are in the majority.
beats.p: It does not mean you are stupid. You were up against arithmetic that is rarely shown to anyone. This site cannot put you among the {kept}, and nobody honest can promise to.

ch07.outroP: The 9% Club is a provocation about arithmetic. It is not a strategy, and there is nothing here to join.
ch07.assumptions: Sources: SEBI's study of individual traders in equity derivatives, July 2025 (press release 39/2025), for FY25, April 2024 to March 2025. These figures cover F&O only, not all investing. SEBI's later study, published in August 2026, reports FY26: {fy26Pct}% of individual traders lost money, with net losses of {fy26Loss} crore. It also revises FY25 to {fy25RevisedPct}% and {fy25RevisedLoss} crore, after widening its sample of brokers. The 75% figure is from SEBI's September 2024 study of FY22 to FY24. This is education, not advice.

ch08.title:
What actually

works.
ch08.tagline: Not a way to beat the market, and not a promise. Just the most boring thing in this course: the same amount, every month, for a very long time.
ch08.chartAlt: Over 10 years, {put10} put in grows to about {value10} at an assumed {rate}% a year, with most of the growth arriving late

beats.p: A SIP, or systematic investment plan, moves a fixed amount every month into a low-cost fund spread across the whole market. No picking. No round trips. No trading charges again and again.
You have put in {put1}. It is worth about {value1}. Look how boring this is.
{put3} in, about {value3} now. This is the stage where most people get bored and stop.

beats.h: Year 5. The grey is still doing the work.
beats.p: {put5} in, about {value5} now. Nearly everything you can see on the chart is money you put in yourself.

beats.h: Year 8. The line starts to lift.
beats.p: {put8} in, about {value8} now. The growth is starting to earn growth of its own, and that is all compounding is.
You put in {put10}. The other {growth10} is growth, {growthShare10}% of the pile, and most of it came late. A real path would not be this smooth: Chapter 06 shows what one looks like.
Change the amount and the years. Notice which one matters more.

calc.disclaimer: Illustration only. Assumes a steady {rate}% a year, which no real investment delivers. Market returns can be lower or negative, and past returns do not guarantee future ones. Mutual fund investments are subject to market risks.

ch08.outroP: Nothing in this chapter needs you to be right about a price. It needs time, a small cost and not stopping. It can still go badly over the years you happen to choose, and nobody can promise otherwise.
ch08.assumptions: Instalments are paid at the end of each month. The {rate}% a year is an assumption chosen to show the shape of compounding. It is not a forecast, a target or a measured historical return. Fund expenses, charges on selling, tax and inflation are left out. No fund is named or recommended. This is education, not advice.

ch01.title:
Who buys

your token?
ch01.tagline: Your tokens came from two friends at a cart. A real share cannot change hands that way. This chapter follows {wallet} through the pipes of the Indian market, before any charge touches it.
ch01.mapAlt: A loop of four stops: your bank, the broker, the exchange and your demat account

beats.h: You cannot walk up to the counter.
beats.p: The cart's ₹3,400 stays in the cart's story. Now picture selling to someone you have never met, or buying a piece of a company 1,000 km away. The counter resets to {wallet}, and this is the way in.
You open an app and add {wallet} over UPI or IMPS. The money leaves your bank account. Nothing has been bought yet.
The app belongs to a broker, a licensed middleman. You tap Buy and it passes your order on. It is the way in, not the place your shares live.

beats.h: The exchange is where orders meet.
beats.p: NSE and BSE are India's two main exchanges. Buyers and sellers never see each other here: orders are matched automatically, by a system you never touch.

beats.h: Your shares land in a vault.
beats.p: The money goes on to the seller. The shares come back to your demat account, held at a depository, CDSL or NSDL. They usually arrive by the next working day.
The bank holds money. The broker carries orders. The exchange matches them. The depository holds the shares. Remember that vault: taking shares out of it is where a charge in Chapter 04 comes from.
A stranger, whose order met yours. You never learn their name. You only ever agree on one thing: the price.

ch01.outroP: It is not inside the app. It sits in a demat account in your name, and the app is one door to it.
ch01.handoffQ: You agreed a price with a stranger. Who set it?
ch01.handoffP: Not the company, and not SEBI. That is Chapter 02.
ch01.assumptions: Simplified. Clearing corporations sit between the exchange and the depository to guarantee the trade, and money can also move by other routes. Delivery trades on NSE and BSE settle on the next working day. This is education, not advice.

ch02.title:
Who decides

the price?
ch02.tagline: Not the company. Not SEBI. A share's price is just the last number where an impatient buyer and an impatient seller agreed.
ch02.bookAlt: An order book with buyers on the left at {bids} and sellers on the right at {asks}

beats.p: Many people picture the company or SEBI updating a number every second. Neither does. Zoom into Stop 3 from Chapter 01 and you find a queue, called the order book. This one is invented, to show how it works.

beats.h: Buyers line up, wanting it cheap.
beats.p: {bids}. Each is an offer: I will pay this much, no more. The best one is {bestBid}.
{asks}. Each is an offer too: I will sell at this price, no less. The best one is {bestAsk}.
The best buyer stops at {bestBid}. The best seller starts at {bestAsk}. That {spread} between them is the spread, and while it stays open, everyone just waits.
Someone wants out now and drops their price to {match}, for {qty} shares. That is lower than any other seller, and still nobody has traded.
You are the impatient buyer. Your order meets theirs and the two clear each other. {deployed} of your {wallet} is now in shares, and the last traded price is {match}.

beats.h: That is all a price is.
beats.p: Not what a share is worth. Not what it should be. Just the last deal two strangers made. The next deal can be different, seconds later.

ch02.outroH: Every price on a screen is a past deal.
ch02.outroP: It tells you where two people last agreed. It does not tell you where the next two will.
ch02.handoffQ: Thousands of deals a day. How do you read them?
ch02.handoffP: Your {qty} shares are about to live through a whole day. That is Chapter 03.
ch02.assumptions: An invented order book, with no real share behind it. Real books hold thousands of orders and match them in milliseconds. A trade fills at the price of the order already waiting, which is why someone had to come down to ₹100 here. Charges are left out until Chapter 04. This is education, not advice.

ch03.title:
Reading

a chart.
ch03.tagline: Trading screens look like a language you were never taught. They are not. One day of your {qty} shares is enough to read all of them.
ch03.dayAlt: The price line for one day, building a single candle from {open} open to {close} close
ch03.rowAlt: A row of {days} candles, one for each day, ending on your day

beats.p: The line on the left is the price through one invented day. The mark on the right is a candle, which starts as nothing but that first number: the open.

beats.h: By mid-morning it has dipped to {low}.
beats.p: Your {qty} shares fall with it, so the counter drops to {lowMoney}. The candle grows a thin line downwards, called a wick. It records the lowest point of the day, for good.
The counter touches {highMoney}. The wick stretches up to mark the high. The candle now remembers how far the day travelled in both directions.
The thick body runs from the open to the close. Teal means it closed higher than it opened. The wicks stay behind as the day's extremes. Four numbers, one shape.

beats.h: Close lower, and the candle turns.
beats.p: Open at {redOpen}, close at {redClose}: same shape, opposite colour. A candle cannot tell you why it happened. Only what happened.

beats.h: A chart is a row of days.
beats.p: Your day is the last of these {days}, all invented. Each candle is one more day compressed into four numbers. That is everything a chart is: a diary of past deals.

beats.h: A diary cannot read the future.
beats.p: These shapes record what buyers and sellers already did. They do not say what happens next, and they leave out something else entirely: what the trade cost you.

ch03.outroP: A chart stops being intimidating once you know it is only a compressed diary. It is still only a diary.
ch03.handoffQ: You saw ₹2,000 become {closeMoney}. Is that what you would keep?
ch03.handoffP: No. There are charges the chart never shows. That is Chapter 04.
ch03.assumptions: Invented prices, with no real share behind them. The market hours shown are the NSE and BSE regular session. The counter values your {qty} shares at the current price and leaves out charges, which arrive in Chapter 04. This is education, not advice.

doubts.heading: Still have a doubt?
doubts.note: Common questions, answered in advance. This is education, not advice.

ch00.q: In the story you got 2% of the profit. Do real companies send you cash like that?
ch00.a: Not automatically. A company's board can choose to pay part of its profit as a dividend, and each share gets the same amount. Many keep most of it to run and grow the business. The cart story simplified this: your slice can rise in value without any cash reaching you.

ch00.q: Can I lose more than the ₹2,000 I put in?
ch00.a: Not by buying shares with your own money. The lowest a share can go is zero, so the most you can lose is what you paid. That changes with borrowed money or futures and options, which Chapter 07 comes to.

ch00.q: If I own 2%, can I tell the company what to do?
ch00.a: You get a vote at shareholder meetings, in proportion to your shares. With a tiny slice your vote will rarely decide anything, and you have no say in daily decisions.

ch00.q: Why did Aarti and Imran sell pieces instead of taking a loan?
ch00.a: A loan has to be repaid with interest, even in a monsoon. Selling ownership brings in money with nothing to repay, but the founders now share every future profit. Real companies weigh the same trade-off.

ch01.q: What happens to my shares in CDSL if my broker app shuts down tomorrow?
ch01.a: They stay yours. Your shares are recorded in your name at the depository, CDSL or NSDL, and a broker shutting down does not make them the broker's property. You would move them to a demat account with another broker, which can take time and paperwork. Cash sitting with the broker is a separate matter, and getting it back can take longer.

ch01.q: Is money in a broker app the same as money in my bank?
ch01.a: No. It is a balance with a broker, not a bank deposit, so bank deposit insurance does not cover it. If a broker fails, the exchanges run investor protection funds, but those have limits and claim rules.

ch01.q: Why can't I buy directly on NSE without a broker?
ch01.a: Only exchange members can place orders on NSE or BSE. A broker is a member, and it also checks your identity and your money before your order goes in. That is why every trade starts at a broker, and why brokers can charge for it.

ch01.q: Why do shares take a day to reach my demat?
ch01.a: Share trades in India settle on the next working day, called T+1. That time goes to moving money and shares between both sides through the clearing system. Your app may show the shares before they actually reach your demat.

ch02.q: If a company announces good news, doesn't it raise its own price?
ch02.a: Not directly. The company changes nothing on the screen. News changes what buyers will pay and what sellers will accept, and the order book moves with them, sometimes within seconds.

ch02.q: What is the difference between a market order and a limit order?
ch02.a: A market order takes the best price waiting right now, so buying at market in this book would have cost {bestAsk}. A limit order names your price and waits, as the seller at {match} did. One is sure to fill but not sure of its price. The other is sure of its price but may never fill.

ch02.q: Can a price go anywhere, any time?
ch02.a: Not without limits. Exchanges set price bands on many shares, which cap how far they can move in a day, and the whole market can pause after a sharp fall. These slow a move down. They do not prevent a loss.

ch02.q: Is a ₹100 share cheaper than a ₹1,000 share?
ch02.a: Not from that number alone. A price is one slice, and companies cut themselves into very different numbers of slices. What the whole company is valued at is its price multiplied by its number of shares. A low price does not mean a bargain.

ch03.q: Can patterns in candles tell me what happens tomorrow?
ch03.a: Not reliably. A candle records what already happened. The research behind this course tested four classes of trading strategy on Indian shares after costs, with four negative results, and the one positive result turned out to be a single stock.

ch03.q: Why are candles on my app green and red, not teal?
ch03.a: Colours are only a convention. Most apps use green for a day that closed higher and red for lower. This course uses its own teal and brick. The shape means the same either way.

ch03.q: Is one candle always one day?
ch03.a: No. A candle can cover five minutes, a day, a week or a month. It always holds the same four numbers for that period, so check the timeframe before reading anything into a chart.

ch03.q: Why does a price sometimes open far from yesterday's close?
ch03.a: News does not wait for 9:15. Orders build up overnight and the first trades of the day reflect them. That jump is called a gap, and it shows as space between one close and the next open. The invented row in this chapter leaves it out for simplicity.

ch04.q: If an app advertises zero brokerage, why did {total} still get cut?
ch04.a: Because {total} is not the zero-brokerage figure: it includes {brokerage} of brokerage from the broker in this example. Remove that and about {noBrokerage} would still go, if the DP charge stayed at {dp}. Zero brokerage removes one cut. STT, exchange charges, stamp duty and GST remain, and DP charges vary by broker.

ch04.q: Do I pay the DP charge if I buy and just hold?
ch04.a: No. It comes when you sell and shares leave your demat. Buying does not trigger it, which is why the same charge hurts someone who sells often far more than someone who rarely sells.

ch04.q: Would two ₹500 trades be cheaper than one {trade} trade?
ch04.a: No, worse. Two separate ₹500 round trips in different shares cost about {twoHalves}, against {total} for one of {trade}, because each carries its own flat charges.

ch04.q: Intraday trades have no DP charge. Are they cheaper?
ch04.a: On that one line, yes: shares bought and sold the same day never reach your demat. But charges are only part of it. SEBI's study of FY23 found that 71% of individual intraday traders in the cash segment lost money.

ch05.q: So is it impossible to start with {c2000}?
ch05.a: No. This chapter measures trading, not owning. The gap applies to every round trip, so {pct2000}% once is very different from {pct2000}% every week. How often you sell changes the sum more than people expect. This is arithmetic, not a recommendation.

ch05.q: What if my broker charges a lower DP fee?
ch05.a: The gap shrinks, but it does not vanish. Even with no DP charge at all, this {c2000} round trip would still need about {gapNoDp}%. DP fees differ by broker, so the charges page is worth reading before comparing apps.
Close, and slightly low. It assumes you sell at the price you bought at. Selling higher raises the sell-side charges a little, so the true figure sits just above it. Tax on any gain is extra.

ch05.q: Does the share's price change the gap?
ch05.a: No. One share at {c2000} and 20 shares at ₹100 cost the same {cost2000} to trade, because charges depend on the total amount, not on the number of shares.

ch06.a: Large Indian companies, left unnamed so that nothing here reads as a tip. How the list was made matters more: it uses companies that are large today, so ones that failed are missing. That makes the result look better than anyone in 2019 could have expected.

ch06.q: Does holding always recover like this?
ch06.a: No. This is one crash. Others have taken many years to recover, and a single company can fall and never come back. Spreading money across many companies reduces that risk. It does not remove it.

ch06.q: Could I have sold before the fall and bought back at the bottom?
ch06.a: Only with hindsight. Nobody knew 24 March 2020 was the bottom, and for {fallDays} days nothing signalled when the fall would stop. Doing this means being right twice: about when to leave, and about when to return.

ch06.q: What was the steep fall around 2023 on the chart?
ch06.a: Mostly one holding. The basket was never rebalanced, so one share grew far too large inside it and then crashed. That is why this chapter teaches from 2020: the 2023 fall says more about how this basket was built than about the market.

ch07.q: Does SEBI's FY25 figure of 91% apply to long-term mutual fund SIPs too?
ch07.a: No. That study counts individual traders in equity derivatives, meaning F&O. It says nothing about mutual funds, SIPs or simply owning shares. Those carry their own risks, which Chapters 06 and 08 come to, but this number is not about them.

ch07.q: Do the 9 keep winning year after year?
ch07.a: It is not a lasting group. SEBI's study of FY22 to FY24 found that only about 7.2% of individual F&O traders made a profit over those three years.

It is the FY25 figure from SEBI's July 2025 study, and the one this site is named after. SEBI's August 2026 study reports {fy26Pct}% for FY26, with net losses of {fy26Loss} crore, and revises FY25 to {fy25RevisedPct}% and {fy25RevisedLoss} crore after adding brokers to its sample. SEBI warns that fewer people traded in FY26, so the lower share is not a sign that trading got easier.

ch07.q: How much did a typical trader lose?
ch07.a: About ₹1.1 lakh on average in FY25. An average hides a wide spread: some lost far less and some far more.

ch08.a: No. It is an assumption for showing the shape of compounding. A real fund's return changes every year, can be negative, and depends on the years you happen to pick. Nobody can promise it.
Yes. If the market is down when you need the money, you can get back less than you put in. A SIP spreads your buying over time. It does not protect you from a fall.

This site does not name or recommend any fund. What anyone can compare is what a fund holds and its expense ratio, the yearly cost taken from your money. For personal advice, SEBI registers investment advisers. This chapter cannot be one.

ch08.q: What if I miss a month or stop?
ch08.a: What you already put in stays invested, and a SIP can usually be paused or stopped. The figures here assume every instalment arrives, so gaps lower them, and early instalments count most because they have the longest to grow.

about.description: Who made The 9% Club, and why: a plain course on what trading actually costs.
about.title: Who made this, and why
about.who: The 9% Club was made by Tanish Jain, a student developer.
about.why: Most beginners learn about the stock market from hype: reels, tips and screenshots of big wins. Very little of it shows the arithmetic underneath, like the charges taken from every trade, or what a real crash felt like for someone who held on.
about.how: This course tries to show that arithmetic instead. Every number on the site comes from a real cost model or from real historical data, and the methodology page says where each one comes from.
about.not: It is education, not advice. It will not tell you what to buy, and nothing here can put anyone among the 9 in 100 who made money. The aim is only to help you see the costs and risks clearly, before you decide anything for yourself.

methodology.description: Where every number on The 9% Club comes from: the cost model, the 2020 crash data and SEBI's studies.
methodology.title: Where every number comes from
methodology.lede: Nothing on this site is a guess presented as a fact. Each figure comes from one of the sources below, and anything invented or assumed is labelled where it appears.
methodology.costs: Chapters 04 and 05 use a cost model for a delivery trade on NSE. It counts brokerage, STT, exchange transaction charges, the SEBI turnover fee, stamp duty, GST and the DP charge. It is a port of a Python cost engine, and automated tests check it against a fixed reference file to six decimal places. For example, a ₹1,000 round trip comes to {total}.
methodology.costsRates: Statutory rates were checked in November 2026. Brokerage and the DP charge use a conservative reading of one discount broker's published fees, so your own contract note may differ.
methodology.costsFixture: The reference file it is tested against
methodology.drawdown: Chapter 06 uses the real price history, from 2019 to 2025, of an equal-weight basket of 49 large Indian companies, bought in January 2019 and never rebalanced. From its high on 11 February 2020 it fell {fallPct}% in {fallDays} days, to 24 March 2020, and took {recoverDays} days to get back. The companies are not named, so nothing here reads as a tip.
methodology.sebiScope: Chapter 07 uses three studies by SEBI, the market regulator. They count individual traders in equity derivatives, meaning F&O, and nothing else: not mutual funds, and not simply owning shares.
methodology.sebiJul2025: July 2025, for FY25 (April 2024 to March 2025): {lost}% of individual traders lost money, with net losses of {loss} crore after charges. Chapter 07's grid and headline tell this FY25 story.
methodology.sebiAug2026: August 2026, for FY25 and FY26: in FY26, {fy26Pct}% lost money, with net losses of {fy26Loss} crore. The same study revises FY25 to {fy25RevisedPct}% and {fy25RevisedLoss} crore, after widening its sample of brokers. SEBI cautions that fewer people traded in FY26, so a smaller share of losers is not a sign that trading got better.
methodology.sebiSep2024: September 2024, for FY22 to FY24: {sep2024Lost}% of individual traders lost money over the three years, only {sep2024Profit}% made a profit over that period, and more than {sep2024KeptTrading}% of loss-makers kept trading after consecutive years of losses.
methodology.prices: All real price data on this site is historical, from 2019 to 2025, more than 30 days old, and used for education only. The order book in Chapter 02, the trading day in Chapter 03 and the steady return in Chapter 08 are invented or assumed, and each is labelled as such on its page.
methodology.simplificationsLede: These are the footnotes from each chapter, shown here word for word.
methodology.mistake: If a number looks wrong, I would like to know.

privacy.description: What The 9% Club stores on your device and what its analytics record, described plainly.
privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.lede: This page describes what the site actually does, checked against its code.
privacy.storedTitle: What is stored on your device
privacy.storedLede: Nothing is stored when you simply read. Two things can be saved, and only after you use a control:

stored.theme: Remembers light or dark mode, after you use the theme button. It stays until you clear this site's data.
stored.locale: Remembers English or Hindi, after you switch language, so the site opens in that language. It is a session cookie, deleted when you close the browser.

privacy.storedNothingElse: There are no other cookies and nothing else in browser storage. The site's fonts are served from this site, not from a third party.
privacy.analyticsWhen: On the live site, page views are counted with Vercel Web Analytics. Preview versions and copies running on someone's own computer collect nothing.
privacy.analyticsHow: According to Vercel's documentation, it does not use third-party cookies. It identifies a visit by a hash of the incoming request, and that visitor session is discarded after 24 hours. It may record these details with each page view:

analyticsPoints.time: the time of the page view
analyticsPoints.query: filtered query parameters in the address
analyticsPoints.location: a rough location: country, region and city
analyticsPoints.os: your device's operating system and its version
analyticsPoints.device: the type of device: mobile, tablet or desktop
analyticsPoints.version: the version of the analytics script

privacy.analyticsSource: Vercel's documentation on Web Analytics privacy
privacy.hosting: The site is hosted on Vercel, which handles the requests your browser makes to load it.
privacy.portfolioLink: The "Built by Tanish" link in the footer adds ?ref=9percentclub to its address, so the author's portfolio site can see that a visit came from here.
privacy.noneTitle: What the site does not do
privacy.none: There are no accounts, no forms and no ads. The calculators run in your browser and send nothing anywhere. Nothing is sold or shared.
